papers.title: Spatial Clonal Discordance in Early Mycosis Fungoides Revealed by Compartment-specific TRBC1 Immunohistochemistry.
papers.authors: Huang C, Shao X, Zang J, Wang H, Song H, Zhang Y, Chen H.
papers.journal: The American journal of surgical pathology
papers.abstract: Diagnosis of early mycosis fungoides (MF) is hindered by overlap with benign dermatoses and by the variable sensitivity of conventional polymerase chain reaction-based molecular clonality assays in paucicellular specimens. We demonstrate that T-cell receptor β-chain constant region 1 (TRBC1) immunohistochemistry (IHC) provides a spatially resolved assessment of T-cell clonality that may aid the evaluation of early MF. In early MF, we identified a characteristic "spatial clonal discordance," where monotypic TRBC1 expression is confined to intraepidermal T cells while dermal infiltrates remain polytypic. This compartment-specific pattern reflects neoplastic epidermotropism and may help explain discordant clonality results obtained by bulk molecular assays in paucicellular lesions. Conversely, tumor-stage MF and Sézary syndrome exhibited spatially concordant, pan-compartmental restriction. Digital image analysis showed high concordance between single-stain IHC and multiplex immunofluorescence, establishing TRBC1+ thresholds of ≤25% or ≥75% for defining clonality. Although this study is limited by its retrospective, single-center design and relatively small cohort, the findings establish TRBC1 IHC as a powerful, spatially informative tool. It effectively overcomes the "dilution effect" of reactive cells in early MF, serving as a high-sensitivity adjunct to conventional molecular testing for accurate, compartment-specific clonal evaluation.
papers.summary: The researchers showed that a stain called TRBC1 can spot the cancer‑related T‑cells in early mycosis fungoides by highlighting them only in the skin’s outer layer, while the deeper layer still looks normal. This “spatial clonal discordance” helps explain why DNA‑based tests often miss the disease in early, cell‑sparse lesions, and suggests TRBC1 staining could be a sensitive add‑on tool for diagnosing early CTCL.

papers.title: The tumour microenvironment in mycosis fungoides - decoupling biological and clinical responses.
papers.authors: de Masson A, Battistella M, Guenova E, Papadavid E, Vermeer MH, Moins-Teisserenc H.
papers.abstract: The tumour microenvironment (TME) plays a pivotal role in the progression of mycosis fungoides (MF), characterised by a shift in the immune response from a T helper (Th) 1 cell (Th1) to a Th2 cell profile. While this framework captures key features of disease progression, recent single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies have further illuminated diverse malignant T-cell states, immune trajectories and spatial niches that extend beyond cytokine polarity alone. Skin-directed and systemic therapies for MF affect both malignant T-cells and the surrounding TME. The therapeutic response begins with biological changes in the TME, including tumour T-cell elimination via tumour cell killing and apoptosis, along with modification of the inflammatory milieu. Because these biological changes take time, early signs of clinical improvement may be subtle. Skin-related treatment-related adverse events, including inflammation, may occur and can be difficult to distinguish from ongoing disease. Given this overlap, careful clinical evaluation is warranted before changes to therapy are considered. It is therefore important to distinguish biological responses in the skin TME from clinical responses on the skin. In this article, we review data on biological and clinical responses to treatment in patients with MF and highlight the lack of biomarkers correlating with skin responses. Finally, we explore emerging tools and consider their potential to improve clinical decision-making when differentiating between biological and clinical responses.
papers.summary: The article reviews how the skin’s immune environment changes during treatment for mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, and explains that these biological shifts—like killing of malignant T‑cells and altered inflammation— often happen before visible skin improvement. Because early treatment effects can look like side‑effects or ongoing disease, doctors need better markers to tell true biological response from clinical appearance, and new technologies may help make those distinctions.

papers.title: CD200 Expression in Folliculotropic Mycosis Fungoides Emerging During Dupilumab Treatment.
papers.authors: Tamaki M, Kusano H, Miyagaki T, Honda R, Aida S, Morimura S, Takekoshi T, Shiomi T, Hamada T, Sugaya M.
papers.abstract: Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides (FMF) or mycosis fungoides with folliculotropism (MF-F) is increasingly recognized in patients initially diagnosed with atopic dermatitis (AD) who subsequently worsen during dupilumab therapy. We report a case of FMF that became clinically apparent after dupilumab treatment. A 47-year-old man with a long-standing diagnosis of AD developed persistent facial plaques and tumors despite treatment with dupilumab. Histopathological examination revealed folliculotropic infiltration of atypical lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gene rearrangement, leading to a diagnosis of FMF. To explore the role of CD200, immunohistochemical staining was performed in the present case, six additional FMF or MF-F cases (two diagnosed during dupilumab treatment and four without dupilumab treatment history), and four AD cases. Strong CD200 expression was detected in the tumor cells of the present case and in both additional MF cases diagnosed during dupilumab therapy. In one case, CD200 expression was observed exclusively in the facial tumorous lesion but not in an erythematous lesion on the trunk. Among four FMF or MF-F cases without dupilumab exposure, only one showed CD200 positivity in a tumorous lesion on the face. In contrast, CD200 expression was absent in all AD cases, regardless of dupilumab treatment history. These findings suggest that CD200 expression may be associated with a subset of folliculotropic MF lesions, particularly tumorous lesions and cases that become clinically apparent during dupilumab treatment.
papers.summary: Researchers looked at a type of skin lymphoma that can appear in people who were first treated for eczema with dupilumab, a drug that blocks certain immune signals. They found that the cancer cells in these cases often show high levels of a protein called CD200, especially in facial tumors, while normal eczema skin does not. This suggests CD200 could be a marker for this lymphoma subtype that emerges during dupilumab therapy.

papers.title: Management of advanced mycosis fungoides and Sézary Syndrome: International Recommendations for systemic treatments and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation from the European Hematology Association, the EORTC Cutaneous Lymphoma Tumours Group, the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphoma, and the Lymphoma Working Party of the EBMT.
papers.authors: Onida F, Quaglino P, Scarisbrick J, Sureda A, Hodak E, Papadavid E, Alberti-Violetti S, Bagot M, Cerroni L, Goyal-O'Leary A, Stadler R, Willemze R, Zain J, Ardigò M, Berti E, de Masson A, Duarte RF, Foss F, González-Barca E, Guitart J, Ortiz-Romero P, Pileri A, Porcu P, Prince HM, Rozati S, Rupoli S, Vermeer MH, Whittaker S, Pimpinelli N, Zinzani PL.
papers.abstract: Advanced mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS) are the most aggressive forms of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and remain associated with a poor prognosis and heterogeneous therapeutic approaches. Recent advances, including targeted therapies and improved transplant strategies, have substantially expanded treatment options, highlighting the need for updated international guidance integrating dermatologic, hematologic, and transplant perspectives. An international multidisciplinary panel convened by the European Hematology Association (EHA), the EORTC Cutaneous Lymphoma Tumours Group (EORTC-CLTG), the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphoma (ISCL), and the EBMT Lymphoma Working Party reviewed the available evidence and developed consensus recommendations for the management of advanced MF and SS. Thirty international experts participated in the process. Recommendations address diagnostic work-up, systemic therapies, treatment sequencing, combination strategies, and indications for allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT). The consensus supports a stage-adapted and compartment-oriented therapeutic approach. Immunomodulatory strategies remain central in advanced CTCL: extracorporeal photopheresis is commonly used as first-line therapy in SS and in patients with significant blood involvement, while interferon-α and retinoids are widely used in MF, often in combination with skin-directed therapies. Mogamulizumab and brentuximab vedotin represent key options after prior systemic therapy, with differential activity across skin, blood, and nodal compartments. Combination approaches integrating systemic and skin-directed treatments may improve response depth and durability. Practical treatment algorithms for advanced MF and SS are proposed to support therapeutic sequencing and multidisciplinary management. Allo-HCT remains the only potentially curative treatment and should be considered early in selected patients with high-risk disease features.
papers.summary: The panel of international experts updated guidance for treating the most aggressive skin‑based T‑cell cancers—advanced mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome—by reviewing evidence on drugs, combination regimens, and stem‑cell transplants. They recommend tailoring therapy to disease location (skin, blood, nodes), using immune‑modulating treatments like photopheresis, interferon‑α or retinoids first, then targeted agents such as mogamulizumab or brentuximab vedotin, and reserving allogeneic stem‑cell transplantation for high‑risk patients as the only potentially curative option.

papers.title: Immune checkpoints inhibitors in the treatment of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Toubasi A, Al-Sayegh TN.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: Background: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare but catastrophic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) caused the JC virus (JCV). However, no effective treatments have been identified. Immune check point inhibitors (ICIs) are considered a potential treatment option. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool the data from the literature that evaluates the efficacy of using ICI in the treatment of PML. Methods: The search was conducted on January 24, 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Embase. Studies were included if they included patients with PML and evaluated the efficacy of using ICIs including PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 inhibitors in PML treatment. The exposure of interest was the use of ICI in the treatment of PML. The outcomes of interest were survival, disability and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) viral load. Rate and weighted mean difference (WMD) and their 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) were used as the effect size in the analysis. Results: We included a total of 186 patients with PML from 52 articles. The survival rate among the included patients was 62% (95%CI: 52%-72%). There was no significant difference in disability between before and after the treatment with ICI (WMD =- 0.03; 95%CI: - 2.11-2.04). On the other hand, the treatment was associated with lower viral levels in the CSF (WMD = 69.20; 95%CI: 1.69-136.70). Conclusions: Future randomized clinical trials or comparative observational studies that investigate the efficacy of using ICI in the treatment of PML compared to other treatment modalities are needed.
papers.summary: The abstract you provided examines immune‑checkpoint inhibitors for a rare brain infection (PML), not cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, so it isn’t applicable to CTCL.

papers.title: Synergistic antibiotic activity and integrated genomic-metabolomic profiling of patch- and plaque-derived Staphylococcus aureus in mycosis fungoides.
papers.authors: Straub FA, Serbin LK, Barkani IE, Grünewald C, Mailänder V, Dominelli N.
papers.abstract: Mycosis fungoides (MF), the most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, is frequently associated with skin dysbiosis, and advanced lesions are often dominated by multidrug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. To characterize microbiologically relevant properties of MF-associated S. aureus, we evaluated synergistic antibiotic combinations and performed integrated phenotypic, genomic, and metabolomic profiling. Several antibiotic combinations, most notably carbenicillin combined with either gentamicin or levofloxacin, exhibited pronounced synergistic activity and restored in vitro antimicrobial activity against highly resistant isolates. Comparative genomic analyses revealed substantial variability between isolates in resistomes and virulence repertoires, including enterotoxins, immune-evasion, and stress-response factors. Metabolomic profiling further revealed isolate-specific extracellular signatures, including putrescine and urocanic acid. In summary, this study identifies promising antibiotic combinations against multidrug-resistant S. aureus strains. Furthermore, this exploratory investigation demonstrates phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity among MF-associated S. aureus isolates, warranting further evaluation in larger longitudinal studies. Importance: Despite its predominance in advanced mycosis fungoides (MF) lesions, the role of multidrug‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus in adverse clinical outcomes remains poorly understood. Bridging the gap between clinical observations and microbiological mechanisms is essential to clarify how S. aureus persists in MF skin and to identify therapeutic alternatives for S. aureus‑positive patients, for whom treatment options remain limited. This study addresses two major clinical needs: the lack of effective antibiotic strategies and the limited understanding of bacterial factors that may contribute to worsened clinical outcomes. By integrating synergistic antibiotic testing with genomic, phenotypic, and metabolomic profiling, our work highlights clinically relevant heterogeneity among MF-associated S. aureus isolates. These findings identify promising therapeutic directions and establish a framework for future large-scale longitudinal studies to better understand the role of diverse S. aureus strains in MF pathogenesis.
papers.summary: The researchers tested combinations of antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus bacteria taken from early‑stage (patch) and later‑stage (plaque) skin lesions of mycosis fungoides, finding that pairing carbenicillin with either gentamicin or levofloxacin dramatically improved killing of strains that were otherwise resistant to many drugs. Genetic and chemical analyses showed that these bacterial isolates differ widely in the genes and metabolites they carry, including toxins and stress‑response factors, suggesting they may influence disease severity in different ways. The work points to specific drug combos that could help treat resistant S. aureus infections in CTCL patients and highlights the need for larger studies to understand how bacterial diversity affects the disease.

papers.title: FoxP3+ Regulatory T-Cells in Canine Cutaneous Lymphoma and Their Role in Immune Modulation.
papers.authors: Semolin LMS, Anai LA, Jark PC, Munhoz TD, Cruvinel GG, Bitencourt RC, DA Rosa Sobreira MF, Camplesi AC, Leitão JR, Santana AE, Alves CEF.
papers.abstract: Background/aimRegulatory T cells (Tregs) are immunosuppressive lymphocytes that maintain immune homeostasis but may also facilitate tumor immune evasion. Their role in canine cutaneous lymphoma (CCL) remains insufficiently understood. We hypothesized that dogs with CCL would exhibit increased Treg levels in both peripheral blood and tumor tissue, thereby contributing to local and systemic immune modulation. Our objective was to evaluate Treg levels in blood and skin of dogs with CCL compared with healthy controls.Materials and methodsTwenty-four dogs were enrolled: 12 with T-cell cutaneous lymphoma confirmed by histopathology and immunohistochemistry and 12 clinically healthy controls, recruited from a veterinary teaching hospital population. In this prospective study, circulating Tregs were quantified by flow cytometry, and FoxP3+ cells in skin were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Statistical analyses included t-tests, non-parametric tests, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.ResultsDogs with CCL had significantly higher circulating Tregs than controls (10.84±1.18% vs. 5.67±0.89%, p=0.0021). FoxP3+ cells were detected exclusively in neoplastic skin (mean, 8.27±5.71%), with no labeling in healthy skin (p=0.0007). No significant differences were observed between epitheliotropic and non-epitheliotropic subtypes. Treg levels and the Treg/CD8+ ratio were not associated with survival outcomes (p>0.20).ConclusionDogs with CCL demonstrated increased Tregs in both peripheral blood and intratumorally, suggesting a role of these cells in CCL-associated immunomodulation. Although Treg levels were not prognostic in this cohort, their accumulation highlights potential therapeutic targets in veterinary oncology.
papers.summary: The study measured a type of immune‑suppressing cell called regulatory T‑cells (Tregs) in the blood and skin of dogs with cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma and compared them to healthy dogs. Dogs with the cancer had about twice as many Tregs circulating in their blood and in the tumor tissue, indicating these cells may help the tumor evade the immune system, though their numbers didn’t predict how long the dogs survived. This suggests that targeting Tregs could be a future treatment strategy in veterinary lymphoma.

papers.title: Human leukocyte antigen loss as a mechanism of immune escape after allogeneic stem cell transplantation in a patient with mycosis fungoides.
papers.authors: Rautenberg C, Metzdorf J, Heinold A, Schneider A, Heinemann FM, Livingstone E, Tapken H, Mohring A, Hadaschik E, Kröger N, Reinhardt C, Arrieta-Bolanos E, Wobser M, Fleischhauer K, Schroeder T.
papers.abstract: Not available.
papers.summary: The report describes a patient with mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, who received an allogeneic stem‑cell transplant (donor‑derived blood‑forming cells). After the transplant, the cancer cells stopped displaying certain human leukocyte antigens (HLA), the proteins that help the immune system recognize and attack abnormal cells, allowing the disease to evade immune attack. This loss of HLA may be a key way the lymphoma can escape the graft‑versus‑tumor effect after transplant.

papers.title: Targeted and Immune-Based Therapies in Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.authors: Bai JQA, Wen S, Chu N, Geng RSQ, Gniadecki R, Piguet V.
papers.abstract: Importance: Advanced cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs), including mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS), are associated with substantial morbidity and limited durable treatment options. Although several targeted and immune-based therapies have emerged, their comparative efficacy, durability, and safety have not been comprehensively synthesized. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of targeted and immune-based monotherapies for CTCL and characterize subtype-specific outcomes in MF and SS. Data sources: MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL databases were searched from inception to April 10, 2026. Study selection: Studies reporting efficacy or safety outcomes in patients with CTCL treated with targeted or immune-based monotherapy were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Data extraction and synthesis: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) reporting guidelines were followed and risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute tool. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled overall response rates (ORRs) with 95% CIs. Main outcomes and measures: Pooled ORR; secondary outcomes were duration of response, progression-free survival, time to response, treatment-related adverse events (AEs), grade 3 or greater AEs, treatment discontinuations, recurrence, and subtype-specific response rates. Results: The analysis included 41 studies comprising 1660 patients with a mean (SD) age of 61.6 (12.6) years; of the 1460 with reported sex, 647 were female (44.3%) and 813 male (55.7%) individuals. Pooled ORRs varied across therapeutic cohorts, led by brentuximab vedotin (69%; 95% CI, 62%-75%; n = 510), interferon alfa (68%; 95% CI, 32%-90%; n = 59), alemtuzumab (65%; 95% CI, 45%-80%; n = 96), mogamulizumab (45%; 95% CI, 35%-56%; n = 514), denileukin diftitox (39%; 95% CI, 33%-46%; n = 341), and pembrolizumab (34%; 95% CI, 20%-51%; n = 33). Among MF cohorts, pooled ORRs ranged from 38% to 66% across evaluated therapies. Among SS cohorts, pooled ORRs ranged from 60% to 74% across evaluated therapies. Sample-size-weighted means of study-reported median duration of response ranged from 4.7 to 9.4 months across reported therapies, while median progression-free survival ranged from 14.4 to 23.3 months. Grade 3 or greater AE rates varied across therapies, ranging from 15% (95% CI, 11%-21%) with mogamulizumab to 26% (95% CI, 7%-64%) with denileukin diftitox. Conclusions and relevance: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, targeted and immune-based therapies demonstrated clinically meaningful activity in CTCL, although important differences existed in response rates, response durability, and toxic effect profiles across therapeutic cohorts. Therapeutic activity also varied according to disease subtype, highlighting the importance of individualized treatment selection. These findings support incorporating disease subtype, anticipated durability of response, and toxicity considerations into treatment decision-making for patients with CTCL.
papers.summary: The review pooled data from 41 studies of 1,660 patients with advanced cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma to compare how well single‑agent targeted or immune‑based drugs work and how safe they are. Overall response rates (the proportion of patients whose disease shrank) were highest for brentuximab vedotin (about 69 %) and interferon‑α (≈68 %), while drugs like pembrolizumab and denileukin diftitox showed lower rates (34‑39 %); responses tended to last 5‑9 months and serious side‑effects occurred in roughly 15‑26 % of patients, varying by drug. The authors conclude that treatment choice should be tailored to the specific CTCL subtype (mycosis fungoides vs. Sézary syndrome), expected durability of benefit, and each drug’s toxicity profile.

papers.title: Characterising the genomic landscape of two clinical risk groups in CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders with cutaneous involvement: a multi-institutional retrospective study.
papers.authors: Biral LPA, Russell V, Selim MA, Roth C, Love C, Shingleton J, Owusu D, Batra A, Mason EF, Kovach A, Amador C, Koff JL, Jaye D, Cheng CL, Evans A, Pillai R, Leppä S, Hsi ED, Ondrejka S, McKinney M, McCall CM, Bettoney S, Sojitra P, Evens A, Behdad A, Galvez C, Fedoriw Y, Thacker E, Thakkar D, Parker C, Happ L, Czader M, Gulati R, Naresh KN, Dave SS, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Background: CD30+ T cell lymphoproliferative disorders (CD30+ T LPD) with cutaneous involvement comprise a diverse group of neoplasms with variable clinical outcomes. The molecular mechanisms underlying the prognostic differences in these diseases are poorly understood. Methods: In this multi-institutional retrospective study, 79 patients with CD30+ T LPD were evaluated. DNA and RNA sequencing were performed on skin biopsy samples to characterise molecular features. Patients were assigned to low- and high-risk groups based on treatment recommendations in clinical records. Pathogenic pathways, immune microenvironments, transcriptomic profiles, driver mutations, and mutation signatures were compared between the risk groups. Findings: Across risk groups, there was high mutational recurrence in genes involved in epigenetic regulation and intracellular signalling pathways. Mutational signature analysis revealed a shared prevalence of 5-methylcytosine deamination, UV exposure, defective mismatch repair, and POLE-associated proofreading deficiency. In contrast, gene set enrichment analysis showed that the high-risk group was enriched in pathways governing cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and immune activation compared to the low-risk group. Furthermore, immune microenvironment deconvolution showed a higher abundance of resting dendritic cells in the low-risk group. Finally, high-risk patients exhibited significant overexpression of clinically relevant proteins, highlighting potential alternative treatment approaches for this population. Interpretation: Mutation analyses suggest diverse pathogenesis in these diseases. The high-risk and low-risk groups diverge in gene expression profiles and immune microenvironment, suggesting that these biological differences hold prognostic significance. Molecularly informed therapeutic strategies should be investigated prospectively through clinical trials. Funding: This work was supported by developmental funds of the Duke Cancer Institute as part of the P30 Cancer Center Support Grant. Data generation was supported in an unrestricted fashion by the NIH, Data Driven Bioscience, Amazon and Google. SSD was supported by the Wellcome Trust Foundation and the NIH.
papers.summary: Researchers sequenced DNA and RNA from skin biopsies of 79 patients with CD30‑positive T‑cell skin cancers and split them into low‑ and high‑risk groups based on how doctors treated them. They found that while both groups shared common mutations affecting gene regulation and signaling, the high‑risk tumors showed more activity in pathways that drive cell division, DNA damage repair, and immune activation, and they had fewer resting dendritic immune cells. These molecular differences could help predict outcomes and point to new, targeted therapies for the higher‑risk patients.

papers.title: Dynamic stratum corneum ceramide alterations reflect barrier dysfunction and clinical response to topical chlormethine treatment in early-stage mycosis fungoides.
papers.authors: Mergen C, Wind SS, Beljaards ESM, Rijneveld R, van Schaick M, Bouwstra JA, Jansen MAA, Klarenbeek NB, Niemeyer-van der Kolk T, Vreeken RJ, van Smeden J, El Ghalbzouri A, Hankemeier T, Quint KD, Vermeer MH, Rissmann R, Rousel J, Next-Generation ImmunoDermatology Consortium (NGID).
papers.abstract: Early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF), a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presents as patches and/or plaques with an impaired skin barrier. The stratum corneum (SC) lipid matrix is important for skin barrier function. Alterations in the SC ceramide profile have been linked to a reduced barrier function in benign inflammatory skin diseases and might also be an underlying factor in the impaired barrier function in MF. Therefore, we characterized barrier function and SC ceramide profiles in lesional and non-lesional skin of 21 patients with early-stage MF and 10 healthy controls, and assessed how these barrier and ceramide characteristics evolve during chlormethine gel treatment in patients. Barrier function was measured by transepidermal water loss. SC ceramides were collected by tape stripping and analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Local inflammatory markers were measured in suction blister fluid. At baseline, MF lesions showed impaired barrier function accompanied by distinct changes in the SC ceramide profile, including altered ceramide subclass composition and reduced ceramide chain length. These abnormalities occurred in the context of a predominantly type 1-skewed inflammatory milieu. Importantly, ceramide alterations were dynamic and improved in patients with a clinical response to chlormethine gel treatment, alongside reduced lesion severity and local inflammation. Longitudinal associations of ceramide characteristics with barrier function, clinical lesion severity, and inflammatory markers support SC ceramide alterations as dynamic correlates of MF disease activity. Together, these findings suggest that SC ceramide alterations may reflect a downstream consequence of inflammation that is shared across inflammatory dermatoses.
papers.summary: The study measured how the skin’s outer‑most layer (the stratum corneum) and its key lipid — ceramides — are altered in early‑stage mycosis fungoides and whether these changes improve with topical chlormethine gel. Researchers found that MF lesions have a leaky barrier and abnormal, shorter‑chain ceramides, which normalize as patients respond clinically to the gel, alongside reduced inflammation. This suggests that ceramide patterns track disease activity and could serve as a marker of treatment response.

papers.title: Large-scale integrated single-cell analysis reveals molecular subtypes and microenvironmental remodeling in cutaneous T cell lymphoma
papers.authors: Reis RJ, Mou E, Liu V, Brunner PM, Borcherding N, Jabbari A.
papers.abstract: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL) comprises a clinically and molecularly heterogeneous group of skin-homing non-Hodgkin lymphomas for which robust biomarkers remain limited. Prior single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have provided important insights into CTCL biology, but many of these prior studies have been limited by small sample sizes and focused on niche questions of interest. Additionally, many studies have suffered from pseudoreplication, resulting in inflated test statistics and reduced external validity. Here, we assembled and integrated scRNA-seq data spanning 244 unique samples and 132 patients across CTCL, healthy control (HC), and benign inflammatory dermatoses (BID) conditions, generating the most diverse atlas of CTCL to date. Following identification of malignant cell populations and heterogeneous, within-sample gene expression alterations, we applied pseudobulk aggregation and robust linear mixed-effects modeling to nominate recurrent changes across this highly heterogeneous patient cohort. Interrogation of the skin microenvironment identified significant compositional and cell type-specific expression changes in CTCL lesions as compared to control lesions and across clinical stages of disease. Finally, we used unbiased clustering to identify stable, molecularly defined subtypes of disease that were predictive of outcome in an independent dataset. Together, this study provides a rigorous analysis of the most diverse scRNA-seq dataset of CTCL ever compiled, nominating specific alterations in cell type composition and gene expression across malignant cell and microenvironmental populations with significant clinical implications.
papers.summary: Researchers combined single‑cell gene‑reading data from 244 skin samples—including patients with cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, healthy people, and those with non‑cancerous skin inflammation—to create the largest detailed map of this cancer’s cells and their surroundings. They found distinct molecular “subtypes” of the lymphoma, each linked to different patterns of immune‑cell changes in the skin and to patients’ outcomes, suggesting new ways to predict prognosis and target therapy.

papers.title: Transformed mycosis fungoides: Biological heterogeneity, clinicopathological features, and prognostic determinants.
papers.authors: de Castro E Souza B, Sanches JA.
papers.abstract: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. A subset of patients develops large cell transformation, a biological and histopathological event associated with advanced-stage disease and poor outcomes. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the biology, clinicopathological features, prognostic factors, and therapeutic implications of transformed MF. Available data indicate that transformation reflects clonal evolution accompanied by genomic instability, dysregulated oncogenic signaling, and gene-expression signatures consistent with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. The most consistently reported adverse prognostic factors include advanced clinical stage, older age, elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase, and absent or low CD30 expression, while emerging biomarkers such as GATA3 may further refine risk stratification. Although treatment generally follows the principles of advanced MF, localized radiotherapy, CD30-directed therapy, and early consideration of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation have particular relevance. Future advances will depend on biomarker-driven risk stratification and prospective studies dedicated to transformed MF.
papers.summary: The review looks at why some cases of mycosis fungoides, the most common skin T‑cell lymphoma, turn into a more aggressive “large‑cell” form, describing the genetic changes and immune‑suppressing environment that drive this transformation. It finds that patients who are older, have more advanced disease, high blood levels of lactate dehydrogenase, or low CD30 protein on their tumor cells tend to do worse, while new markers like GATA3 may help predict risk. The authors suggest that, beyond standard advanced‑stage therapy, targeted radiation, CD30‑focused drugs, and early stem‑cell transplant can be especially useful for these high‑risk patients.

papers.title: Multimodal Imaging-Assisted Diagnosis of a Rare Primary Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma Secondary to Imatinib plus Sintilimab in a Postoperative GIST Patient
papers.authors: Chen Y, Zhong H, Deng W, Wang R.
papers.abstract: Background: Primary cutaneous T cell lymphoma represents a heterogeneous subgroup of extranodal non‑Hodgkin lymphoma and frequently presents with non‑specific cutaneous manifestations that contribute to high rates of misdiagnosis. Emerging evidence suggests combined treatment with tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors and PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors may drive secondary lymphomagenesis. This case adds to literature by highlighting the diagnostic value of multimodal non‑invasive skin imaging (dermoscopy plus high‑frequency ultrasound) as ancillary clues before definitive histopathological confirmation. Case Summary: A 58‑year‑old male with completely‑resected high‑risk gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) developed progressive generalized skin lesions following imatinib and single‑dose sintilimab therapy. He presented with widespread purplish‑red scaly papules and plaques accompanied by pruritus, eyebrow loss and palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests revealed mild monocytosis and slight anaemia. Multimodal imaging including high‑frequency ultrasound and dermoscopy identified characteristic cutaneous changes. Histopathology together with immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of primary cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. Unfortunately, the patient was lost to follow‑up after hospital discharge, so post‑discharge therapeutic response could not be evaluated. Conclusion: Multimodal non‑invasive skin imaging assists early suspicion of PCTCL; definitive diagnosis still depends on histopathology and immunohistochemistry. Clinicians should remain alert for secondary cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders among patients receiving combined targeted‑immune anticancer therapy.
papers.summary: A 58‑year‑old man who had surgery for a gut tumor and was treated with the drugs imatinib (a tyrosine‑kinase inhibitor) and sintilimab (a PD‑1 immune‑checkpoint blocker) later developed widespread itchy, purplish‑red skin bumps and loss of eyebrows. Using a combination of dermoscopy (magnified skin surface imaging) and high‑frequency ultrasound helped doctors suspect a rare skin T‑cell lymphoma before confirming it with a tissue biopsy. The case shows that non‑invasive skin imaging can flag such secondary cancers early, but a definitive diagnosis still requires microscopic analysis of the skin.

papers.title: Mogamulizumab efficacy on the skin compartment of cutaneous T-cell lymphomas based on longitudinal analysis.
papers.authors: Nakano N, Murotani K, Ohya Y, Nishio Y.
papers.abstract: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is staged by the degree of skin, lymph node, viscera and blood involvement. Skin response is a determinant of treatment decisions. Mogamulizumab, an anti-CC chemokine receptor 4 antibody, is approved for mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome after ≥1 systemic therapy. Longitudinal changes in modified Severity-Weighted Assessment Tool (mSWAT) score, and cluster of differentiation (CD)4+CD7-/CD26- cell subsets during mogamulizumab treatment were investigated as an exploratory post-hoc analysis. While chronological differences in mSWAT scores were not interpreted by a linear mixed model (LMM) due to a statistically significant interaction term, significant differences based on responses in CD7- (-690.5/μL; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1195 to -186.2; p = 0.0076) and CD26- (-1029/μL; 95% CI, -1705 to -353.7; p = 0.0030) cell counts were identified. Actual values of mSWAT scores decreased for responders at Week (W) 12 and 24 from baseline (BL) (mean ± standard error: BL: 97.57 ± 6.52; W12: 52.34 ± 6.16; W24: 34.89 ± 4.93) following a rapid decrease of CD7- cells in blood at W4 (BL: 2809 ± 650.3/μL; W4: 204.4 ± 50.76/μL; W12: 101.9 ± 28.81/μL; W24: 152.8 ± 54.98/μL). Monitoring both blood and skin improvements is important for effective mogamulizumab treatment in patients with advanced stage disease.
papers.summary: The study tracked how skin disease severity (measured by a scoring system called mSWAT) and abnormal T‑cell subsets in the blood changed over time in patients with advanced cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma treated with mogamulizumab, an antibody that targets the CCR4 receptor on cancer cells. It found that patients who responded to the drug showed a rapid drop in abnormal CD7‑ and CD26‑negative T cells in the blood, which was followed by a marked reduction in skin lesions by weeks 12–24. The authors suggest that watching both blood markers and skin scores together helps gauge how well mogamulizumab is working.

papers.title: The role of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in adults with mature T-cell lymphomas.
papers.authors: Stocker LD, Thielecke L, Schmitz C, Monsef I, Skoetz N, Herling M.
papers.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
papers.abstract: Rationale: Mature T-cell lymphomas (MTCL) are a rare, heterogeneous group of malignancies that arise from post-thymic T-lymphocytes, with a generally poor prognosis. For a long time, the standard therapy for most MTCL subtypes has been polychemotherapies. Hopes to prolong overall survival in MTCL have been associated with transplant procedures such as high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell transplantation (autoSCT) or allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT). Objectives: To assess the benefits and harms of alloSCT in the treatment of MTCL in adults (≥ 18 years old) compared to any other treatment, particularly with respect to its efficacy and safety as first-line therapy, and secondarily, for its efficacy and safety as a salvage option. Search methods: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, conference proceedings, and two databases of ongoing trials from January 1990 to October 2025 for prospective and retrospective studies evaluating the role of alloSCT for MTCL. Eligibility criteria: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospectively planned trials assessing the role of alloSCT as first-line or salvage treatment for MTCL. As determined at the protocol stage, we excluded retrospective trials because we identified prospective ones. We excluded trials in which less than 80% of participants had MTCL, unless we could obtain a subgroup analysis for these participants. Outcomes: We analyzed overall survival, progression-free survival (PFS), response rate, treatment-related mortality (TRM), quality of life (QoL), grade 3 and 4 adverse events, and incidences of acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD and cGVHD, respectively). Risk of bias: We assessed the risk of bias (RoB) in the included studies using Cochrane's RoB 2 tool for RCTs and the Cochrane Childhood Cancer Group's assessment criteria tool for observational studies. We rated the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach for all previously stated outcomes. Synthesis methods: We followed standard Cochrane methodology, and two independent review authors performed all steps regarding study selection and risk of bias assessment in duplicate. Included studies: We included one RCT of alloSCT as first-line treatment for MTCL (103 participants), and two prospectively planned trials of alloSCT as salvage treatment (119 participants): one Mendelian-randomized controlled trial for cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) (102 participants) and one prospective observational trial for non-cutaneous MTCL (17 participants). We identified three ongoing trials. All of them are non-randomized, phase-II studies. They will mostly include relapsed or refractory lymphomas. Two other studies are awaiting classification. Overall, we rated both included RCTs to have some concerns of bias due to bias arising from the randomization process, and missing outcome data. The RoB for the prospective observational study was rated serious due to the study design, small number of participants, and reporting and detection bias. Synthesis of results: As we did not identify enough RCTs, we did not conduct a meta-analysis. We rated the evidence for all outcomes to be of low to very low certainty, due to the very small number of events and limitations in study design. AlloSCT compared to autoSCT for adults with MTCL (first-line) We included one RCT with 103 participants. AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in little to no difference in two-year overall survival (hazard ratio (HR) 1.3 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.7 to 2.4; low-certainty evidence) or PFS HR 0.9 (95% CI 0.5 to 1.5; low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in a large increase in TRM (RR 18.70, 95% CI 1.11 to 315.72; low-certainty evidence), but may have no effect on overall response rate (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.45; low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT compared to autoSCT may result in little to no difference in the number of adverse events (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.75). 84% of all participants receiving alloSCT had aGVHD and 47% had cGVHD (very low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT for adults with non-cutaneous MTCL (relapsed or refractory setting) We included one phase-II study with 17 participants. Overall survival and PFS at two years were presented graphically in the included study, and were approximately 80% and 64%, respectively (very low-certainty evidence for both). The overall response rate was 76% after one month (70% in complete remission and 6% in partial remission; very low-certainty evidence). The two-year TRM rate was presented graphically in the included study, without making reference to absolute numbers, and was approximately 6% (very low-certainty evidence). 35% of all participants had aGVHD and 41% had cGVHD (very low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were not reported. AlloSCT compared to other treatment for adults with CTCL (relapsed or refractory setting) We included one RCT with 102 participants. AlloSCT compared to any other treatment may make little or no difference to overall survival (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.29; very low-certainty evidence), but may increase PFS (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.69; very low-certainty evidence). AlloSCT may make little or no difference to the number of adverse events (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50; very low-certainty evidence). The one-year cumulative incidence of cGVHD was 31.4% (very low-certainty evidence). The overall response rate and TRM were not reported. Authors' conclusions: In this systematic review, we identified one RCT of alloSCT as first-line treatment for MTCL, and one Mendelian RCT and one prospectively planned phase-II trial of alloSCT for relapsed or refractory MTCL. We encountered difficulties while extracting data from these studies, because there were major differences in study designs, intervention and control groups. We identified low- to very low-certainty evidence on the effectiveness and safety of alloSCT for adults with MTCL. We had some concerns about the risk of bias in the two RCTs and serious concerns about bias in the phase-II study. As there are three ongoing studies evaluating alloSCT, mostly for relapsed or refractory MTCL, it is possible that an update of this review will be published in the near future. However, none of the ongoing studies are of an RCT design. Funding: Department I of Internal Medicine, Center for Integrated Oncology Aachen Bonn Cologne Duesseldorf, Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital Cologne, University of Cologne. Registration: Protocol available via DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD014672.
papers.summary: The review looked at whether giving patients with mature T‑cell lymphomas, including cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, an allogeneic stem‑cell transplant (using donor cells) improves survival compared with standard chemotherapy or autologous transplant (using the patient’s own cells). The limited data, mostly from small trials with low‑certainty evidence, suggest that donor transplants do not clearly boost overall survival and may raise the risk of transplant‑related death and graft‑versus‑host disease, though they might modestly extend the time patients stay disease‑free. More robust, randomized studies are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

papers.title: When response lasts: ORR4 as an On-Treatment Prognostic Marker in Mogamulizumab-Treated Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome.
papers.authors: Stadler R.

papers.title: Conjunctival involvement with corneal extension in pediatric mycosis fungoides. Surgical and immunomodulatory management.
papers.authors: Cárceles Montoya A, Tarazona Jaimes CP, Romero Valero D.
papers.journal: Archivos de la Sociedad Espanola de Oftalmologia
papers.abstract: A 13-year-old boy with mycosis fungoides (MF) presented with uncommon ophthalmic involvement. Clinical examination revealed a vascularized conjunctival nodule with corneal extension involving the visual axis and causing severe visual impairment. Initial treatment with topical corticosteroids and tacrolimus showed poor response. Complete surgical excision was performed for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Histopathological analysis confirmed progression to T-cell lymphoma. Adjuvant treatment with topical interferon alfa-2b was initiated. After two years of follow-up, no recurrence was observed, with partial visual improvement. This case highlights a rare paediatric presentation and central corneal involvement, both infrequently described. Combined surgical and immunomodulatory treatment achieved adequate local control, although residual sequelae limiting visual acuity persisted.
papers.summary: A 13‑year‑old boy with mycosis fungoides, a skin‑based T‑cell lymphoma, developed a rare eye lesion that grew onto his cornea and threatened his vision. After steroids and a drug that suppresses immune activity failed, doctors removed the growth surgically and then applied eye drops containing interferon‑alpha, a protein that boosts anti‑cancer immunity. Two years later the lesion has not returned and his vision has improved somewhat, showing that combined surgery and immune‑modulating eye drops can control this unusual ocular spread.

papers.title: Folliculotropic mycosis fungoides presenting with acneiform lesions, comedones, and alopecia: A diagnostic challenge.
papers.authors: Orts Paco JF, Mallo García S, Rebollo Caballero B.

papers.title: Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of T-Cell Receptor Beta Constant Region 1 and 2 Transcript in Situ Hybridization for Clonality Assessment in Mycosis Fungoides.
papers.authors: Madan V, Lai J, Rozati S, Paul S, Jedrych J.
papers.abstract: Background: Mycosis fungoides (MF) may be difficult to distinguish from inflammatory dermatoses. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement assays provide ancillary evidence of clonality but lack spatial resolution. We evaluated the feasibility of RNA in situ hybridization (RNA-ISH) targeting TCR beta constant isoforms, TRBC1 and TRBC2, in routine skin biopsies. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 15 MF biopsies, predominantly Stage IA-IB, and 11 inflammatory controls using TRBC1 and TRBC2 RNA-ISH on separate sections. Expression was assessed semiquantitatively in matched intraepidermal regions using exploratory thresholds. Available TCR gamma PCR results were reviewed. Results: RNA-ISH was successful in all 26 samples. Nine MF cases (60%) showed TRBC skewing, three (20%) were indeterminate, and three (20%) were double negative. All controls showed balanced polytypic expression. Exploratory sensitivity was 60% (95% CI, 32.3%-83.7%) and specificity 100% (95% CI, 71.5%-100%). Substantial discordance with available PCR results was observed. Conclusions: TRBC1/TRBC2 RNA-ISH is technically feasible in archival skin and can demonstrate spatial isoform skewing in a subset of MF biopsies. Technical and interpretive limitations preclude diagnostic validation; larger multiplexed studies are warranted.
papers.summary: Researchers tested a new lab technique that visualizes two versions of a T‑cell gene (TRBC1 and TRBC2) directly in skin biopsy slices from patients with early‑stage mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. They found that about 60 % of the lymphoma samples showed an imbalance between the two gene versions—a pattern not seen in benign inflammatory skin conditions—suggesting the method can highlight cancerous T‑cells in their tissue context, though it missed many cases and needs further refinement.

papers.title: Patient preferences and travel burden before radiotherapy for primary cutaneous lymphoma: baseline results from the S-MISR registry.
papers.authors: Steike DR, Elsayad K, Falke I, Kandler C, Eich HT.
papers.journal: Strahlentherapie und Onkologie : Organ der Deutschen Rontgengesellschaft ... [et al]
papers.abstract: Purpose: Patients with primary cutaneous lymphoma may have substantial impairments in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and may require referral to specialized radiation oncology centers. The current exploratory baseline analysis assessed patient preferences for quality of life (QoL) versus length of life (LoL), travel distance, and baseline HRQoL before radiotherapy. Methods: Of 130 screened patients, 82 patients with primary cutaneous lymphoma referred for radiotherapy were enrolled in the prospective S‑MISR registry between September 2019 and August 2024. Their QoL-versus-LoL preferences were assessed using the Quality-Quantity Questionnaire. Baseline HRQoL was evaluated using Skindex-29 and EORTC QLQ-C30. Travel distance to the treating radiation oncology department was analyzed overall and by lymphoma subtype. Results: Median age was 63 years (range 34-92), and 59 patients (72%) had advanced-stage disease. Fifty-six patients (68%) had mycosis fungoides (MF), 13 (16%) had Sézary syndrome (SS), and 13 (16%) had other primary cutaneous lymphomas. Overall, 31 patients (38%) prioritized QoL, 21 (25%) prioritized LoL, and 30 (37%) rated both equally. Median travel distance was longest for Sézary syndrome (201 km), followed by mycosis fungoides (114 km) and non-MF/SS lymphomas (65 km). Older age and longer travel distance emerged as potential factors associated with QoL preference. Baseline Skindex-29 scores indicated greater HRQoL impairment in MF and SS than in non-MF/SS lymphomas. Conclusion: Patient preferences regarding QoL versus LoL vary considerably before radiotherapy. Travel burden may be an important patient-centered factor for treatment planning, shared decision-making, and future prospective radiotherapy studies.
papers.summary: Researchers surveyed 82 people with primary cutaneous lymphoma who were about to receive radiation therapy to see how far they were traveling, how they weighed quality of life against length of life, and how badly their skin symptoms were affecting them. About a third of patients said quality of life mattered most, another quarter prioritized living longer, and the rest valued both equally; those who lived farther away—especially patients with Sézary syndrome—were more likely to favor quality of life. The study shows that travel distance and disease type influence patients’ treatment preferences, highlighting the need to consider these factors when planning radiation therapy.

papers.title: Clinical analysis of mycosis fungoides involving the central nervous system：a case report
papers.authors: Qiuxiang W, Huili R, Jun G, Yun X, Jinbo C, Jinhuan X, Dan Y, Hui C.
papers.abstract: Background Mycosis fungoides (MF) with central nervous system (CNS) involvement is a rare complication of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma(CTCL) without unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.We retrospectively analyzed the clinical presentation, diagnostic and therapeutic course, and prognosis of a single case of MF with CNS involvement treated at our institution.Combined neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid flow cytometry suggested CNS infiltration, and stereotactic biopsy, histopathology together with positive T-cell receptor gene rearrangement confirmed the diagnosis.This case indicates high vigilance for CNS dissemination in MF patients with new neurological symptoms. It highlights that CNS involvement should be suspected in MF patients with new neurological symptoms, and combined imaging, cerebrospinal fluid testing and biopsy enables timely diagnosis of CNS dissemination in advanced MF. Case Presentation: We report a 49-year-old male with mycosis fungoides (MF) who developed new-onset left facial hypesthesia and left upper limb weakness. Neuroimaging revealed a right frontal lobe lesion with multiple extracranial hypermetabolic foci. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed aberrant T-lymphocytes, supporting a diagnosis of MF with central nervous system (CNS) involvement. The patient initially responded to systemic chemotherapy but was subsequently complicated by septic shock and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Two months later, follow-up imaging showed new brain lesions; stereotactic biopsy and positive T-cell receptor gene rearrangement confirmed persistent CNS involvement. Conclusions This case highlights that in MF patients presenting with CNS symptoms,the diagnosis of MF with CNS involvement should be considered and an aggressive diagnostic workup, including imageological assessment, lumbar puncture, tissue biopsy and so on, should be pursued to establish a diagnosis. Therapeutic strategies must be individualized based on each patient's specific disease status.
papers.summary: The report describes a 49‑year‑old man with mycosis fungoides, a type of skin‑based T‑cell lymphoma, who developed new neurological problems that turned out to be cancer spreading into his brain and spinal fluid. Advanced imaging, analysis of cerebrospinal fluid, and a targeted brain biopsy confirmed the CNS involvement, showing that doctors should quickly investigate any new neurologic symptoms in MF patients with these combined tests. The case also illustrates that treatment must be tailored individually, as the patient initially responded to chemotherapy but later faced serious complications and recurrent brain lesions.

papers.title: 'The good cancer': communicating a hypopigmented mycosis fungoides diagnosis to families.
papers.authors: Kim E, Santhanagopalan R, Strowd LC, Feldman SR.

papers.title: Inflammatory rheumatic diseases under mogamulizumab: a multicenter series of 11 cases.
papers.authors: Wahler A, Guignard S, Quéreux G, Carpentier O, Marcé D, Dietrich E, Saintvoirin M, Amatore F, Hainaut E, Cumptich MV, Ardiles CB, Dereure O, Beylot-Barry M, Ingen-Housz-Oro S.
papers.abstract: Background: Mogamulizumab (MOGA), an anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody for mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS), can trigger immune-mediated complications, such as rashes or endocrine disorders. Rheumatological manifestations are rare. Objectives: To describe cases of inflammatory rheumatism (IR) induced or worsened by MOGA in MF/SS patients. Methods: A retrospective study collected cases of IR (polymyalgia rheumatica [PMR], rheumatoid arthritis [RA], spondylarthritis, or unclassified IR) in MF/SS patients treated with MOGA across centers of the French Cutaneous Lymphomas Group. Clinical, biological, and imaging data were analyzed. Results: Eleven patients (7 men, 4 women; median age: 72 years) developed IR during (10/11) or soon after (1/11) MOGA treatment. Symptoms included joint pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. All had biological inflammatory syndrome, synovitis on ultrasound, and no autoantibodies. PET-CT confirmed hypermetabolism consistent with intense joint inflammation (SUV=8.0). Management with systemic corticosteroids ± methotrexate led to remission in most cases. MOGA had to be discontinued in 8 patients, with lymphoma control maintained in 6. Conclusions: MOGA may induce disabling IR, potentially via CCR4+ regulatory T-cell depletion. Early recognition and treatment with corticosteroids ± methotrexate are essential, though MOGA discontinuation may be required.
papers.summary: Researchers looked at 11 patients with cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma who were treated with mogamulizumab, a drug that blocks a protein called CCR4, and found that most of them developed new or worsening joint inflammation such as painful stiffness and swelling. The joint problems appeared during or right after therapy, showed up on imaging as active inflammation, and usually improved with steroids (and sometimes methotrexate), although the cancer drug often had to be stopped. This suggests mogamulizumab can trigger serious rheumatic side effects, likely by removing regulatory immune cells, so doctors need to watch for joint symptoms and treat them promptly.

papers.title: Cutaneous Lymphoma International Prognostic Index and Risk Stratification in Advanced Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome.
papers.authors: Roccuzzo G, Bashir A, Evison F, Whittaker S, Bagot M, Guenova E, Papadavid E, Prince HM, Sanches JA, Miyashiro DR, Servitje O, Querfeld C, Akilov O, Arumainathan A, Bennett L, Battistella M, Bayne M, Alberti Violetti S, Fava P, Iselin C, Beylot-Barry M, Busschots AM, Cowan R, Dummer R, Dunnill G, Estrach T, Geskin L, Gru AA, Guitart J, Herrera MC, Hodak E, Horwitz S, Jonak C, Klemke CD, Knobler R, Mckay P, Marschalkó M, Massone C, Matin RN, Mitteldorf C, Novoa R, Ortiz-Romero P, Pimpinelli N, Pujol RM, Rieger KE, Stadler R, Trautinger F, Latzka J, Vermeer M, Wachsmuth R, Weatherhead S, Wehkamp U, Wobser M, Quaglino P, Kim YH, Scarisbrick J.
papers.abstract: Importance: Risk stratification in advanced mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome (MF/SS) remains suboptimal given that current TNMB (tumor, node, metastasis, blood) staging has limited prognostic value for clinically relevant outcomes. Objective: To determine whether the Cutaneous Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (CLIPI) may be used to predict progression-free survival (PFS) and best objective response (BOR) in patients with advanced MF/SS. Design, setting, and participants: This international prospective cohort study included patients with stage IIB to IVB MF/SS from the PROCLIPI trial which ran from July 1, 2015, to May 1, 2025, across 46 referral centers. Median follow-up was 4.75 (95% CI, 4.04-5.13) years; eligible participants had complete data on CLIPI, PFS, and BOR. Data were analyzed from September 1 to December 1, 2025. Exposure: CLIPI score at diagnosis, based on age (>60 years), elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase, N3 nodal status, and large-cell transformation in the skin. Patients were classified as having low (0 or 1 factor), intermediate (2 factors), or high risk (3 or 4 factors). Main outcomes and measures: PFS (defined as diagnosis to disease progression or death) and BOR (complete response, partial response, stable disease, or progressive disease) during follow-up. Exploratory analyses evaluated treatment effects before progression using inverse probability weighting. Results: Among 277 patients (median [IQR] age at diagnosis, 66 [23-89] years; 183 male individuals [65.7%]), 144 (52.0%) were classified as having low risk, 93 (33.6%) intermediate risk, and 40 (14.4%) high risk. They had a median PFS of 4.64 years (95% CI, 3.50-5.76), 2.72 years (95% CI, 1.81-4.56), and 0.89 years (95% CI, 0.65-1.14), respectively (log-rank P Conclusions and relevance: In this international prospective cohort of patients with advanced MF/SS, CLIPI scores were associated with risk of disease progression and likelihood of response beyond clinical stage. These findings indicate that CLIPI may help to refine risk stratification and support its integration into clinical decision-making and future trial design.
papers.summary: The study tested whether the Cutaneous Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (CLIPI)—a score that adds together age over 60, high blood lactate dehydrogenase, extensive lymph‑node involvement, and large‑cell transformation in the skin—can predict how long patients with advanced mycosis fungoides or Sézary syndrome will stay progression‑free and how well they will respond to treatment. In a cohort of 277 patients, those with low CLIPI scores lived about 4½ years without disease worsening, while intermediate and high scores corresponded to roughly 2½ years and less than a year, respectively, and higher scores also meant poorer treatment responses. The authors conclude that CLIPI provides a more precise way to gauge risk than traditional staging and could guide therapy choices and trial designs.

papers.title: Erythrodermic Psoriasis With Anasarca and Lymphadenopathy Mimicking Lymphoma.
papers.authors: Din N.
papers.abstract: A 25-year-old man with chronic psoriasis presented with progressive erythroderma, anasarca with a reported 30-lb weight gain, and bulky lymphadenopathy, raising concern for lymphoma. Lymph node biopsy showed dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, and expert review of skin specimens favored an inflammatory process over cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Low-dose methotrexate was started, followed by patient-reported improvement in function, edema, and skin changes. This case emphasizes recognizing severe inflammatory skin disease as a possible contributor to systemic illness and correlating the clinical presentation with pathology. Improvement after methotrexate supports clinical benefit but is not diagnostic of psoriasis.
papers.summary: A 25‑year‑old man with long‑standing psoriasis developed widespread red skin, severe swelling (anasarca) and large lymph nodes, making doctors worry it might be lymphoma. A lymph node biopsy showed a benign inflammatory change, and skin samples were judged to be due to severe psoriasis rather than a skin lymphoma. Treating him with low‑dose methotrexate improved his skin, swelling, and overall function, showing that aggressive psoriasis can mimic lymphoma and that methotrexate can help even though it doesn’t confirm the diagnosis.

papers.title: Systemic Retinoids in Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma: A Scoping Review of Clinical Use and Evidence Gaps.
papers.authors: Bui T, Niknejad K, Urbanski N, Fidan DG, Wolner Z, Rozati S.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Systemic retinoids are ubiquitously used in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), often in combination with skin-directed or systemic therapies, yet their role within contemporary multimodal treatment strategies has not been comprehensively synthesized. Methods: We conducted a PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review of systemic retinoids in CTCL using PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library through December 1, 2025. Study-level and treatment arm-level analyses characterized treatment patterns, outcomes, and reporting practices. Reported response rates were descriptively summarized after excluding case reports and case series. Results: A total of 141 studies comprising 153 treatment arms and 3805 participants with CTCL were included. Bexarotene was the most frequently studied retinoid (113/153, 73.9%), and combination therapy predominated (100/153, 65.4%). Retinoids were used across the treatment continuum, most frequently in salvage settings (85/153, 55.6%). Among treatment arms with reported stage, advanced-stage disease more frequently incorporated bexarotene-containing combination regimens than early-stage disease (80.7% vs 50.0%; p = 0.017). Among 59 overall response rate (ORR) observations from observational studies and clinical trials, median reported ORR was 60.0% for combination therapy and 51.5% for monotherapy; by individual retinoid, median reported ORRs were 56.6% for bexarotene, 59.5% for acitretin, and 57.0% for isotretinoin. Durability and safety reporting remained inconsistent, with progression-free survival and grade ≥ 3 adverse events reported in only 13.1% and 32.0% of treatment arms, respectively. Conclusions: Systemic retinoids remain versatile and clinically relevant components of contemporary CTCL management. Rather than functioning primarily as standalone therapies, they are commonly incorporated into multimodal treatment strategies across disease stages and therapeutic settings, with reported clinical activity across individual agents and both monotherapy and combination approaches. Heterogeneity across studies precludes comparative efficacy conclusions and underscores the need for standardized response assessment, durability endpoints, and comprehensive safety and demographic reporting.
papers.summary: This review looked at 141 studies on systemic retinoids—drugs that affect cell growth—used to treat cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (CTCL). It found that the most common retinoid, bexarotene, is often added to other treatments, especially for advanced disease, and that overall response rates are about 60 % with combinations and 52 % with single drugs. However, the studies vary widely in how they report outcomes and side‑effects, so it’s hard to say which approach works best.

papers.title: Non-epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in a 5-week-old golden retriever puppy.
papers.authors: Krauter C, Roy G, Chuback C, Koziy R, Fernandez NJ.
papers.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
papers.abstract: A 5-week-old male golden retriever puppy was presented with multiple, rapidly progressive skin masses. One of the masses had been present since birth; the duration of the other 2 masses was unknown. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lesions revealed a monomorphic population of round cells, raising suspicion for a round cell neoplasm. Two representative masses were submitted for histologic examination and immunohistochemical analysis. Histologically, the neoplasm was composed of dense, non-epitheliotropic infiltrates of atypical lymphoid cells within the dermis and subcutis. Immunophenotyping confirmed a T-cell origin, establishing a diagnosis of non-epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. In the postoperative period, the puppy's health declined and humane euthanasia was elected. A postmortem examination did not occur, precluding assessment for systemic involvement. To the authors' knowledge this is the first case of non-epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in a dog of this age documented in the veterinary literature. This report underscores the importance of including cutaneous lymphoma in the differential diagnosis of rapidly progressive skin masses in a dog, irrespective of age, and highlights the utility of histopathology and immunohistochemistry for achieving a diagnosis. Key clinical message: Lymphoma can occur in dogs of any age and should not be excluded as a differential diagnosis, even in very young puppies.
papers.summary: Researchers examined a 5‑week‑old golden retriever puppy with fast‑growing skin tumors and, using tissue microscopy and special staining, identified the growths as a rare type of skin‑based T‑cell lymphoma that does not involve the hair follicles. This is the first reported case of this lymphoma in such a young dog, showing that even very young puppies can develop cutaneous lymphoma and that detailed lab tests are essential for accurate diagnosis.

papers.title: A single-cell atlas identifies oncogenic transcriptional programs and immune escape mechanisms in CTCL.
papers.authors: Wang C, Geng X, Abdelrahman S, Fu Y, Kady N, Rauf MA, Hristov A, Tejasvi T, Murga-Zamalloa C, Tsoi LC, Welch J, Fox J, Carty S, Gudjonsson JE, Wilcox RA.
papers.abstract: Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) are a heterogeneous group of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Outcomes for patients with advanced-stage disease are suboptimal, because few complete and durable responses are achieved with currently available therapeutic agents. However, improved understanding of oncogenic transcriptional programs in malignant T cells and their engagement with the tumor microenvironment (TME) may unveil therapeutic vulnerabilities. Therefore, we have compiled the largest available single-cell RNA-sequencing CTCL atlas that includes >2 million skin and blood cells from 116 individual patients. We identified recurrent transcriptional programs in malignant T cells, a subset of which are associated with GATA binding protein 3-dependent transcriptional programs, especially in the setting of large cell transformation and advanced-stage disease. Many of the transcriptional programs identified are therapeutically targetable with clinically available agents, including HDAC, XPO1, CDK9, JAK/CSF1R, and IKZF1/IKZF3 antagonists. The CTCL TME is dominated by infiltrating and exhausted effector and cytotoxic T cells that are restrained by a robust infiltrate of regulatory T cells, transcriptionally polarized monocytes/macrophages, and cancer-associated fibroblasts. Collectively, these findings have significant implications for the rational design of combinatorial strategies targeting immune checkpoints, including programmed cell death protein 1. We have identified transcriptional programs, driven by oncogenic transcription factors, and constituents of the TME as therapeutic vulnerabilities in CTCL, and hope that the CTCL atlas constructed will provide a valuable resource for future studies exploiting these therapeutic vulnerabilities.
papers.summary: Researchers built the biggest single‑cell map of skin and blood cells from 116 CTCL patients, revealing that malignant T cells repeatedly use certain gene‑control programs—especially those driven by a factor called GATA‑3—in aggressive disease. Many of these programs can be hit with existing drugs (like HDAC, JAK or CDK9 inhibitors), and the tumor environment is packed with exhausted immune cells kept in check by regulatory T cells, altered macrophages and fibroblasts, suggesting that combining immune‑checkpoint blockers (e.g., PD‑1 inhibitors) with those drugs could improve treatment.

papers.title: Case Report: Epitheliotropic cutaneous presentation of multicentric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in a dog.
papers.authors: Kim GH, Ko BG, Kim SH, Seo KW, Youn HY, Ryu MO.
papers.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common histological subtype of canine multicentric lymphoma, whereas epitheliotropism is classically associated with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. A 9-year-old neutered male Chihuahua was diagnosed with stage IVb multicentric lymphoma and achieved complete remission with a UW-25 L-CHOP protocol. However, an upper lip mass, cytologically consistent with lymphoma, developed during remission. Electrochemotherapy was performed for local control and resulted in marked reduction of the lesion. The dog later developed recurrent peripheral lymphadenopathy and multiple progressive cutaneous masses despite various chemotherapy protocols and was euthanized at week 59 because of progressive clinical deterioration. Histopathology confirmed diffuse large cell lymphoma in the submandibular lymph node, whereas the cutaneous lesions showed neoplastic lymphoid infiltration with multifocal epidermal invasion, mimicking epitheliotropic T-cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed diffuse CD20 expression in both sites, with CD3 labeling limited to scattered background lymphocytes. These findings supported the interpretation of secondary cutaneous involvement of DLBCL with a highly unusual epitheliotropic pattern and emphasize the importance of IHC for accurate immunophenotypic classification of cutaneous lymphoma lesions.
papers.summary: The report describes a 9‑year‑old Chihuahua that had aggressive B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) that spread to the skin in a pattern usually seen only in T‑cell skin cancers. The skin lesions showed lymphocytes invading the outer skin layer, but special staining confirmed they were still B‑cells (CD20 positive). This case highlights that B‑cell lymphoma can mimic T‑cell skin disease and that immunostaining is essential for correct diagnosis.

papers.title: SkinNet-X: a task coupled feature interaction framework for joint skin lesion segmentation and classification.
papers.authors: Babu E, Murali S.
papers.abstract: Well trained segmentation and classification of skin lesions from dermoscopic images are crucial to an early detection of melanoma and other malignant skin disease. While many deep learning models reach impressive overall performance, most existing approaches treat segmentation and classification as separate tasks, leading to limited interaction between spatial lesion localization and semantic disease knowledge. This segregation results in a high variance prediction and would reduce the overall robustness of automated diagnostic systems. To mitigate this limitation, we proposed SkinNet-X: a unified multitask framework to reformulate the skin lesion segmentation and classification tasks jointly. We achieve this with a shared hierarchical feature representation to transfer knowledge between both tasks while introducing new Cross Task Consistency Learning (CTCL) strategy that enforces semantic consistency between lesion localization and disease prediction during joint optimization. In order to enhance the discriminative capability of feature expression and alleviate redundant representations, a dual stage multi label feature optimization module is further exploited, accompanied by an adaptive PolyLoss based optimization strategy stabilizing multitask learning. The effectiveness of the proposed SkinNet-X framework was evaluated using segmentation and classification experiments on the ISIC 2018, ISIC 2019, and HAM10000 benchmark datasets. We also performed additional analyses, namely ablation studies, computational complexity evaluation, sensitivity analysis and statistical validation to explore the contribution of each architectural component. Experimental results show that the proposed multitask learning strategy can consistently improve accuracy of lesion localization and performance of classification with robust generalizability across multiple datasets. These findings demonstrate that SkinNet-X is an effective and potentially useful framework for automated skin lesion analysis and computer-aided dermatological diagnosis.
papers.summary: SkinNet‑X is a new computer‑vision system that simultaneously marks the exact shape of a skin lesion and predicts what type of skin cancer it might be. By letting the two tasks share information and enforcing that the location of the lesion matches the disease prediction, the model reduces errors and works reliably on several large skin‑image datasets. The study shows that this joint approach improves both the accuracy of lesion mapping and the correctness of cancer classification compared to methods that treat the two problems separately.

papers.title: Immune-related adverse events with mogamulizumab in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: A multicentre study.
papers.authors: Neubauer D, Palassin P, Ram-Wolff C, Masson A, Delaleu J, Kottler D, Amatore F, Adamski H, Bejar C, Janela-Lapert R, Guenova E, Bernard P, Lheure C, Machet L, Troin L, Quereux G, Pham-Ledard A, Faiz S, Grange F, Corre YL, Nikkels A, Barete S, Manea L, Amazan E, Maria AT, Moulis L, Dereure O, Samaran Q, Groupe Français d'Étude des Lymphomes Cutanés (GFELC).
papers.journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
papers.abstract: Background: Mogamulizumab, an anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody used in advanced mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sezary syndrome (SS), also depletes regulatory T cells, potentially leading to immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Unlike mogamulizumab-associated rash (MAR), other irAEs remain poorly documented to date. Objectives: To estimate the prevalence of mogamulizumab-associated irAEs (excluding MAR), characterize their clinical profile and assess management strategies and outcome. Methods: A retrospective nationwide multicentre survey was conducted using the French Study Group on Cutaneous Lymphomas (GFELC) database with standardized questionnaires collecting demographic, clinical and therapeutic data. An exploratory pharmacovigilance analysis was also performed using the WHO pharmacovigilance database, VigiBase. Results: Among 403 treated patients from 19 participating centres, 34 patients (8.4%) experienced at least one irAE (41 events overall, event rate 10.2%). The most frequent irAEs involved the endocrine system, skin, and liver. Severe (grade ≥3) or serious irAEs occurred in about one-third of cases, resulting in permanent treatment discontinuation in 29%. Most events occurred after several months of treatment, often in patients experiencing objective responses. In VigiBase (2464 reports), reported irAEs were most frequently digestive, musculoskeletal, cutaneous, and hepatic. Conclusions: In this large retrospective series, a minority of patients developed irAEs during mogamulizumab treatment, although a substantial proportion were rated as severe and led to permanent treatment discontinuation. These findings highlight the need for systematic detection, as with immune checkpoint inhibitors, early recognition and prolonged monitoring, as irAEs may occur late during treatment. Prospective studies are warranted to refine epidemiological data along with diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
papers.summary: A study of 403 patients with advanced cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma treated with the drug mogamulizumab found that about 8 % developed immune‑related side effects other than the usual rash. The most common problems involved the endocrine system, skin, and liver, and roughly one‑third of these events were severe enough to stop treatment permanently. The findings suggest that doctors should monitor patients closely for late‑onset immune reactions, just as they do with other immune‑boosting cancer drugs.

papers.title: Early Progression with Nodal Involvement Is a Predictor of Early Mortality in Mycosis Fungoides: A Retrospective, Registry-Based Cohort Study.
papers.authors: Filippatos C, Fotiou D, Briasoulis A, Ntanasis-Stathopoulos I, Terpos E, Gavriatopoulou M.
papers.abstract: Nodal involvement is a key indicator of advanced disease in mycosis fungoides (MF). While progression within 24 months is prognostic of survival in other indolent lymphomas, such clinical benchmarks in MF remain underexplored.
